newsitem.title: INDIA: YEAREND - Indian commodity futures still a far cry.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Indian commodity futures still a far cry.

text.p: India, despite strenuous efforts to open its economy in recent years, has developed cold feet on introducing commodities futures trading due to the conflicting interests of its coalition government, analysts said on Friday.
They said the government, run by a centre-left grouping of 13 political parties, lacked the political will to introduce futures trading in a country whose economy is still mainly agriculture-based.
"Futures trading in commodities is not a priority for the present government. Its main concern is survival," said Bombay Sugar Merchants' Association president Mohan Gurnani.
An official committee has recommended the introduction of futures trading in cotton, oilseeds and silver.
Forward trading in gold may be permitted later and sugar could be considered a fit case if existing price and supply controls were removed, the committee said.
At present, futures trading is allowed in castorseed, hessian, gur (jaggery), potatoes, turmeric and pepper.
Forward trading in most Indian commodities was banned in the 1950s and 1960s in a bid to stabilise prices and end speculation and hoarding.
"As far as sugar is concerned, the sooner they open it the better for the sugar economy," Gurnani said. "Because we are in a surplus situation."
"But the question is whether it will be permitted. My answer is no, not with this government." he said.
An Agriculture Ministry official said the proposal for commodities futures trading was only at "the loud thinking level" and nothing concrete had emerged.
Political economists share that view.

"I don't think there is any thinking in the government (about bringing in futures trading)," said Jagdish Shettigar, an economist with India's main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
"So far no such indication has come, nor is it debated," he said. "Concept-wise, I welcome this, specially keeping in mind the interest of Indian traders."
Officials said a proposal to introduce futures trading in cotton had been awaiting approval by the federal cabinet for some months.

"I have my reservations. India's agriculture minister is a communist. Communists regard forward trading as a capitalist instrument and speculative," said Indian Cotton Mills' Federation secretary M.P. Gajaria.
Traders said the government could be concerned that its pro-farmer image would be damaged if market economy measures like forward trading were introduced.

"We consider that forward markets are more transparent and and more liquid," said an official of the East India Cotton Association (EICA). "In forward markets, prices are determined purely on the basis of supply and demand."
In cotton trade, forward markets offered considerable benefit to all market functionaries, including farmers, merchants, exporters, importers and consumers, he said.
"Futures trading will safegaurd the country's interest in terms of prices," BJP's Shettigar said.
Traders said they feel frustrated about the government's delay in permitting futures trade, saying it is a logical sequel to market reforms the previous administration had started.

"With the opening of our economy to global economic forces and competition, our export and import trade in commodities has been facing new problems and new challenges," said Bombay Oilseeds and Oils Exchange president Navin Shah.
"One feels utterly frustrated by the total lack of any positive response to the need for permitting and actively promoting futures trading in commodities," he said.

Shah said most agricultural commodity markets were undergoing a period of fairly high price volatility, creating risks in the market which affected farmers, traders, industry and the economy at large.
"Farm commodities are not only subject to the vagaries of the weather and market, but also of government policies," Shah said.
"Unless India acts fast, it will miss the most scientific and modern instrument called forward trading as the country steps into the 21st century," he added.
